title: In your light we will see light
author: Psalms
lines: How precious is your loving kindness, God!
The children of men take refuge under the shadow of your wings.
They shall be abundantly satisfied with the abundance of your house.
You will make them drink of the river of your pleasures.
For with you is the spring of life.
In your light we will see light.
why: Plato said the Good is like the sun: by its light we see everything else. The psalmist, centuries earlier and in another world, said the same of God, and added what Plato did not: that this light is loving kindness, a shelter and a feast. Learn it to carry both thoughts together: we do not see the light by our own power, but by the light itself.

title: One who rules his spirit
author: Proverbs
lines: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty;
one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.
why: Plato divided the soul into reason, spirit and appetite, and said a person is just when reason rules. Israel's wise men had put it in one line: the hardest city to take is yourself. Learn it for the moment anger rises, and remember that the victory that matters is the one nobody sees.

title: Until philosophers are kings
src: Plato, Republic V, 473c–d · tr. Benjamin Jowett (1871)
author: Plato
lines: Until philosophers are kings,
or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy,
and political greatness and wisdom meet in one,
and those commoner natures who pursue either to the exclusion of the other are compelled to stand aside,
cities will never have rest from their evils,—
nor the human race, as I believe,—
and then only will this our State have a possibility of life and behold the light of day.
why: The most famous and most argued-over sentence in the Republic. Plato expected laughter, and got it, and worse: some readers have heard in it the voice of every ruler who claimed to know best. Learn it to hold both thoughts: power without wisdom ruins cities, and those who claim wisdom must still answer to the people they rule.

title: Both are dear, but truth comes first
src: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.6 · tr. D. P. Chase (1847)
author: Aristotle
lines: Still perhaps it may appear better,
nay to be our duty where the safety of the truth is concerned,
to upset if need be even our own theories,
specially as we are lovers of wisdom:
for since both are dear to us, we are bound to prefer the truth.
why: Aristotle studied under Plato for twenty years, and here he begins to take apart his teacher's theory of the Good. He says he does it reluctantly, because the theory belongs to friends, but truth comes before friends. The Middle Ages shortened it to a proverb: Plato is my friend, but truth is a greater friend. Learn it for any argument with someone you love.
